data.title: Salary gaps challenge employers heading into 2027
data.description:
Reeracoen expects selective pay investment as employers balance recruitment budgets with workers’ expectations.

Employers face a mismatch between salary expectations and recruitment budgets heading into 2027, with 80.3% of hiring managers identifying pay expectations as a hiring challenge, according to Reeracoen.

The recruitment firm’s Singapore Salary & Hiring Guide 2026/2027 expects companies to remain selective, concentrating compensation spending on business-critical roles and capabilities that are harder to recruit.

Its research involving 375 Singapore hiring managers highlights the pressure employers face when competing for talent.

Separate employee research involving 337 respondents found that 47.5% considered base salary the single most important factor when choosing a job. Another finding showed that 58.8% would consider changing jobs for higher pay.

Reeracoen said employers needed to identify where uncompetitive compensation was restricting recruitment and where other elements of an offer could influence candidates’ decisions.

The guide pointed to improving hiring sentiment alongside continued caution over wage increases.

In July 2026, 48.7% of firms planned to hire over the following three months, whilst 27.9% expected to raise wages, according to Ministry of Manpower data cited in the report.

These figures describe near-term expectations in 2026 rather than confirmed plans for 2027.

Reeracoen’s employer watchlist identifies five priorities for the coming year: targeted hiring, salary expectations, skills mismatches, AI and skills readiness, and retention beyond pay.

It recommended comparing salaries with external market benchmarks rather than relying solely on a company’s historical pay levels.

Employers should also distinguish skills required immediately from those employees can learn after joining, whilst allowing longer recruitment lead times for specialist engineering roles.

For compensation planning, the guide favoured differentiated spending based on a role’s importance and the scarcity of relevant skills rather than uniform increases.

It also recommended strengthening retention before seeking replacements for difficult-to-fill positions.

Whilst salary remains central to employment decisions, Reeracoen said flexibility, career progression, benefits and manager quality also influence whether employees stay.

The guide presents a selective hiring and compensation outlook but does not forecast a specific salary-growth rate for 2027.

data.title: Singapore signs seven agreements to strengthen air hub
data.description:
The partnerships expand opportunities for airline services and aviation training across several regions.

Singapore has signed three air services agreements and four training agreements to strengthen its international aviation links and support air travel growth.

The agreements were concluded on 18 and 19 November on the sidelines of the seventh Worldwide Air Transport Conference in Montreal, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore said.

Singapore upgraded its air services agreements with Brazil and Türkiye and signed its first such agreement with El Salvador.

Under the updated Türkiye agreement, designated airlines from both countries can operate additional passenger services without restrictions on capacity or aircraft type.

The Brazil agreement further liberalises the air services framework, including cargo operations, and establishes a foundation for potential direct flights as economic activity and exchanges between the countries grow.

The agreement with El Salvador enables connectivity through codesharing on flights via third countries. It also provides the regulatory framework for direct services when commercial opportunities arise.

Singapore and El Salvador currently have no direct passenger services, and the announcement did not include any new direct routes.

CAAS also signed training agreements with the International Civil Aviation Organization, Colombia, Mozambique and the Kyrgyz Republic.

ICAO and the Singapore Aviation Academy will jointly develop a 4.5-day Leaders in Aviation programme for directors-general of civil aviation. It will cover governance, safety and security oversight, sustainability, organisational leadership and resilience.

The other partnerships will support training and professional development for aviation personnel in Latin America and the Caribbean, Central Asia and Africa.

CAAS Director-General Han Kok Juan said Singapore would continue pursuing air services liberalisation to create opportunities for airlines to expand operations and improve travel convenience.

He added that partnerships with ICAO and other states would equip aviation leaders to address emerging challenges and support growing demand.

data.title: Daily Markets Briefing: STI down 2.11%
data.description:
Not a single STI constituent closed in positive territory.

The Straits Times Index (STI) closed at 4,972.230, down 2.11% on Friday, 20 November at 5:21 p.m.

Every STI constituent ended the session flat or in the red, with Seatrium Ltd the biggest loser, down 8.77%, followed by SATS (down 5.29%) and Venture Manufacturing (down 3.32%).

data.title: Mobile wallets hit cross-border barriers despite interoperability push
data.description:
In Africa, users often need a new wallet and KYC verification when crossing borders.

Mobile wallet users in Africa still face restrictions when making payments outside their home countries, highlighting gaps in cross-border payment connectivity despite efforts to improve interoperability.

“If I am Kenyan and go across the border to Tanzania, I cannot use my wallet to make a payment,” said Alvin Okari, managing director for East Africa at Capital Pay International, at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November.

Users often have to register for a new wallet and undergo another know-your-customer (KYC) process when entering a different country. In some cases, wallet access is also tied to the duration of their visa.

He called for regulators to address mobile wallet mobility and enable cross-border merchant acquiring so consumers can use their existing accounts when travelling.

Across East Africa, central banks have mandated interoperability between payment service providers, whilst local switches such as Tanzania's TIPS and Rwanda's R-switch allow providers to connect with multiple banks through a single application programming interface (API).

However, Okari said connecting domestic payment networks is not enough if users cannot access them across borders.

He pointed to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) as a framework that could facilitate digital payments between African countries.

Syed Mohammad Kamal, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh, said wider digital payment adoption also depends on incentives for merchants and consumers.

Merchants may prefer cash because digital transactions involve merchant discount rates (MDR) and make business activity more visible to tax authorities.

“Merchants are comfortable receiving cash nowadays because they are not within the tax net and are not paying anything extra for the MDR,” Kamal said.

He called for stronger incentives to encourage merchants to accept digital payments, alongside greater regulatory enforcement of interoperability.

Kamal also highlighted remittance costs as a barrier to formal payment channels. Bangladesh offers a 2.5% incentive for overseas citizens sending money through official channels, although informal remittance providers remain competitors.

Meanwhile, Stanislav Skvirsky, CEO of payme, cited Uzbekistan's remote identification and open banking regulations as measures that helped expand digital financial services.

The country introduced remote identification in 2016, allowing customers to access financial services without visiting bank branches.

Open banking rules also enabled customers to connect cards from different banks to fintech applications.

Uzbekistan additionally introduced 1% cashback on payments made through digital channels, including cards and mobile wallets.

data.title: MAS clears Ebury Singapore to add currency hedging, e-money services
data.description:
Ebury is a global fintech firm specialising in cross-border payments, amongst others.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore has given Ebury Payments Pte. Ltd. (Ebury Singapore) a Capital Markets Services (CMS) licence and approved a variation of its existing Major Payment Institution (MPI) licence to add account issuance and e-money issuance services.

Ebury expects to offer payment and treasury services to clients in Singapore in the first half of 2027, subject to MAS final approval and conditions.

Once issued, the CMS licence will let Ebury Singapore offer corporate hedging products, such as over-the-counter foreign exchange forwards and options.

Mid-market businesses and regional treasury centres can use them to protect their balance sheets and cash flows from currency swings.

Ebury Singapore is the Singapore arm of Ebury, a global fintech firm specialising in cross-border payments, foreign exchange risk management and financial solutions.

data.title: Payment firms call for regulatory alignment as cross-border links expand
data.description:
Bilateral and multilateral payment links could improve network coverage and resilience across markets.

Payment firms are seeking greater regulatory alignment and interoperability across markets as efforts to connect national payment networks expand across Asia.

Payment firms are calling for greater regulatory alignment and common compliance standards across markets as efforts to connect national payment networks expand across Asia.

Speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival 2026, Shadab Taiyabi, Asia head of fintech sales at HSBC's Global Payments Solutions, said existing payment infrastructure was largely in place, but regulatory differences remained a major source of friction.

"The real friction points sometimes lie in the overall regulation and compliance across the differences that could be there across markets," he said.

He said banks and payment providers needed to work with other players in the financial ecosystem to understand the entire transaction process and deliver smoother services to customers.

For businesses, the challenges extend beyond whether a payment can be made. Taiyabi said customers also consider the cost, timing and certainty of transactions.

Ben Wong, general manager for Southeast Asia and Hong Kong at Adyen, said merchants initially focus on payment costs but become more concerned with transaction success rates and settlement times as they gain experience.

Merchants assess how many transactions are successfully completed out of every 100 attempts, as well as how long it takes for funds to reach them and the currencies in which they can receive payments, he said.

Local regulations can also prevent merchants from processing payments domestically in markets where they operate.

Wong said businesses expanding from Singapore into Japan, for instance, may have to establish local operations before they can process payments locally. This could require them to pay local taxes and hire an operations team.

Violas Xiao, Singapore chief executive of XTransfer, said foreign exchange markups could significantly affect smaller businesses, particularly those with profit margins below 10%.

An FX markup of 3% to 4% could eat into their profits and determine whether a business remains viable, she said.

Some small and medium-sized enterprises in emerging markets also struggle to obtain US dollar liquidity, leaving them with limited alternatives such as informal transfer channels that can charge high fees and expose businesses to the risk of losing their money and goods.

Xiao said SMEs also face difficulties with digital onboarding and transaction monitoring because regulatory requirements differ across jurisdictions and trade documents are often not standardised.

XTransfer has developed in-house optical character recognition technology to read and verify trade documents, helping it detect potential fraud more quickly.

It has also developed 100 AI agents to verify trade documents by reading different languages and formats and checking information against databases covering logistics and customs.

Xiao said the company's monthly compliance cost per active merchant was about US$5.

She called on regulators to standardise licensing processes and risk rules for document tracking, as well as establish protocols for sharing know-your-business and know-your-customer information while protecting data.

Beyond regulatory alignment, executives said connecting national payment networks through bilateral and multilateral arrangements could improve the reach and resilience of cross-border transactions.

Jeremy Tan, founder and chief executive of Liquid Group, said regulatory support had increased over the past 12 to 24 months for linking national payment systems.

Although many systems follow similar transaction formats and standards, connecting more networks will require greater coordination to ensure they operate coherently, he said.

"Most payment systems, even though they are national and they support national payment clearing, a lot of them, most of them, do follow quite common standards," Tan said.

Tan said bilateral links could serve important payment corridors, whilst multilateral networks could extend coverage to markets without direct connections.

He cited Project Nexus, which is designed to facilitate peer-to-peer transfers between Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and India, as an example of a multilateral arrangement that complements existing bilateral links.

Having multiple connections could also make payment infrastructure more resilient, while increasing competition and potentially lowering transaction costs, he said.

“I would like to see a lot more interoperability between payment methods that benefits not just ASEAN, it benefits the whole industry,” said Wong.

HSBC has also launched tokenised deposit services, which represent fiat currency balances on its blockchain.

Taiyabi said the services initially support round-the-clock, instantaneous intra-company treasury payments in Hong Kong, Singapore, the UK, US, Luxembourg and the United Arab Emirates. HSBC has recently expanded the services into other European countries, with the objective of eventually supporting interbank settlements.

HSBC has also completed an interbank transaction using a SWIFT-based blockchain ledger, he said.

Taiyabi said payment companies must maintain bank-grade compliance to remove friction from cross-border transactions. "There is no shortcut to compliance," he said.

data.title: Account takeovers drive 52% of identity fraud in financial services
data.description:
Successful onboarding no longer guarantees account security.

Account takeovers account for 52% of identity fraud in financial services, highlighting the growing risk of fraudsters compromising accounts after customers have passed initial identity checks, according to Entrust.

Minh Nguyen, vice president of product for identity security at Entrust, cited the figure during a panel discussion at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November, where industry executives examined how generative AI is changing identity fraud.

He said financial institutions could no longer treat successful onboarding as proof that an account would remain secure.

“Once the digital identity is issued, you still have risk around account takeover,” Nguyen said, adding that institutions needed to strengthen authentication throughout the customer lifecycle.

He also pointed to social engineering as a growing weakness, as fraudsters increasingly manipulate legitimate customers into accessing their accounts or authorising transactions.

The challenge extends beyond detecting fake identities. Iain Armstrong, executive director of financial crime compliance strategy at ComplyAdvantage, said fraudsters would shift towards authorised push payment scams if stronger identity credentials made account impersonation more difficult.

“Cryptography can potentially tell you who is carrying the telephone and who is making the call, but it can't tell you what that person has been talked into by a fraudster,” he said.

Aishwarya Jayakumar, Visa's head of risk and security intelligence solutions for value-added services in APAC, said banks should combine cyber threat intelligence with fraud monitoring to identify suspicious activity before a transaction takes place.

She also highlighted behavioural signals, including unusual typing patterns, hesitation when entering beneficiary details, and signs that a customer may be receiving instructions during a transaction.

Meanwhile, Yair Tal, CEO of AU10TIX, said generative AI had made it easier for fraudsters to launch coordinated identity attacks at scale, increasing the need for financial institutions to strengthen their verification and monitoring systems.

data.title: Payment firms seek regional links to navigate fragmented systems
data.description:
Merchants are seeking financing, lending, and other financial services through digital payment platforms.

Payment providers are placing greater emphasis on connecting local banking systems and payment networks as businesses operating across Asia seek simpler ways to manage transactions across multiple markets.

Speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival 2026, Anuj Khosla, chief executive of digital business at Hitachi Payment Services, said payment providers were now looking beyond transaction fees for revenue as competition and regulatory pressures squeezed margins.

The industry was shifting towards value-added services, including embedded finance, merchant applications, and consumer financial products, he said. Acquirers, for instance, could offer financing to merchants and earn interest margins and processing fees, rather than relying solely on merchant discount rates.

In India, lenders are using merchants' digital payment records and cash transactions to assess their creditworthiness and offer loans against card receivables, he added.

Khosla said merchants could apply for working capital loans through merchant applications, complete digital know-your-customer checks and sign agreements without visiting bank branches. “They are willing to pay for this user experience, which banks and acquirers are bringing on the table.”

Yukinobu Saeki, managing executive officer and chief executive for Asia-Pacific at MUFG Bank, said companies operating across the region need better visibility and control over their financial operations, including cash positions, liquidity and payments across different markets.

“The challenge is not making the cross-border payment faster. It's of course mandatory, but so it's a complexity of managing different banks or payment systems or formats in each market,” he said.

MUFG Unity connects payments and collections across the bank's partner institutions in Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines, giving corporate clients access to local banking capabilities through one relationship.

Saeki said the bank aims to provide clients with “one single gateway” to its partner banks' networks, allowing them to access local capabilities for payroll, tax and supplier payments.

The service also brings transaction information from MUFG and its partner banks into a more consistent format, helping companies improve visibility and simplify reconciliation.

“This is a real value of our network. That is so connecting the local strengths of our partner banks into a one regional proposition for our clients,” he said.

NTT DATA Japan is also focusing on connecting payment systems across markets through Adaptis, its merchant payment brand operating in Japan, Southeast Asia and India.

Shinichiro Nishikawa, head of global payments strategy and transformation at NTT DATA Japan, said each Southeast Asian market has its own regulations, licensing requirements and consumer payment habits, making it difficult for companies to operate across the region.

He said Adaptis focuses on domestic transactions and settlements, while cross-border transactions require connections with other providers, including MUFG Unity.

Nishikawa said the two services can work together to help businesses transfer money across markets and improve transaction visibility.

He also highlighted the need to simplify connections between local payment systems, particularly when merchants must meet different certification requirements in each country, even when using the same payment terminal.

“Then one single API and one single connection. Then clients can very easily operate in multiple countries,” he said.

Nishikawa added that payment providers must also work with other networks and financial institutions to support cross-border transactions as new forms of financial infrastructure emerge.

Adeline Kim, Visa's group country manager for regional Southeast Asia and senior vice-president for global clients in Asia-Pacific, said the future of payments would depend on providers' ability to connect different networks rather than rely on a single payment system.

She said the industry was moving towards a “network of networks”, in which transactions could move across different systems without consumers or businesses needing to understand the processes involved.

“I don't think the future is going to be on a single rail or a single form of money, whether stable coins versus fiat,” she said.

“The winner is going to be the one who is able to connect to different networks seamlessly,” she added.

Kim cited Singapore's Project BLOOM, which brings together policymakers, financial institutions, digital asset infrastructure, and payment networks to explore applications for digital infrastructure and stablecoins.

Visa is participating in the project, with 24/7 settlement among the use cases it is working on.

Kim said an open ecosystem would allow competition and encourage innovation, whilst giving payment providers opportunities to connect newer forms of money with existing payment systems.

Khosla said India had also made progress in connecting payment infrastructure through its Unified Payments Interface (UPI).

He cited the industry's decision to open UPI rails for Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) acceptance,  giving the digital currency access to more than 60 million merchants.

However, he said the industry was still looking for a compelling consumer use case for CBDCs, as customers could already make payments using their bank accounts through UPI.

Khosla said the experience showed the importance of establishing both merchant acceptance and consumer demand when introducing a new payment product.

Saeki said traditional payment infrastructure and newer digital rails would likely coexist, as they offer different benefits to clients.

Existing systems would remain important for their security, reliability and wider reach, whilst newer solutions could offer benefits such as round-the-clock and programmable settlement.

“It's still too early to say which model will prevail, and a different solution will relatively likely coexist at least for a certain long period,” he said.

He added that banks would need to connect the two systems whilst continuing to improve existing infrastructure and develop new solutions.

data.title: MAS calls for common standards as stablecoin use expands
data.description:
B2B transactions are emerging as a key use case for stablecoins.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is working with financial institutions to establish common standards for using different forms of digital money across institutions and borders, as stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits gain traction in cross-border payments.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November, Leong Sing Chiong, MAS deputy managing director for Markets and Development, said the adoption of digital money will depend on whether it can operate across institutions and jurisdictions under trusted and interoperable arrangements.

“Trusted money requires confidence in its value stability, redemption arrangements, legal treatment, governance, and compliance,” Leong said during a panel discussion.

Leong identified business-to-business transactions as one area where stablecoins are gaining traction, citing companies operating in Singapore that conduct business with counterparts in Central Asia.

He also pointed to the formation of bank consortia around regulated stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits, although he cautioned that greater coordination between financial institutions does not necessarily mean adoption is increasing.

Another development to watch is agentic payments, where AI agents initiate transactions on behalf of users and businesses. “Will this drive payments through card schemes, tokenised bank deposits, or will it favour stablecoins? We have to watch this space closely,” Leong said.

The European Central Bank's Executive Board member Piero Cipollone said the rationale for introducing new payment rails differs across markets.

Europe's digital euro initiative, for instance, is partly intended to reduce dependence on non-European payment providers and provide a common public payment infrastructure.

Cipollone said 13 of the euro area's 21 countries do not have a domestic payment scheme, leaving consumers increasingly dependent on international providers as cash use declines.

“The objective is to give people the freedom to choose how they pay, whether with central bank money, commercial bank money, or other forms of money,” he said.

Meanwhile, Reserve Bank of India deputy governor Swaminathan Janakiraman highlighted the need to strengthen payment system resilience as transaction volumes grow.

India's Unified Payments Interface processed 25 billion payments in the previous month, averaging more than 800 million transactions daily.

He said financial institutions remain responsible for outsourced operations, regardless of how many third parties are involved in payment processing.

“You can outsource a job, but not the responsibility that should lie with the regulated entity,” Janakiraman said.

data.title: Fintech firms rethink cybersecurity as AI advances
data.description:
Executives warn that AI advances could expose payment systems to cyberattacks and erode customer trust.

Financial technology (fintech) executives are raising concerns about cybersecurity as advances in artificial intelligence (AI) increase the risks of attacks on financial systems, with companies facing growing demands to protect their infrastructure and maintain customer trust.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival on 20 November, Tazapay Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Rahul Shinghal said cybersecurity had become a major concern for fintech companies, which already face challenges involving regulatory approvals, scaling operations and cross-border payments.

"Cybersecurity is just top of mind for all of us right now," he said.

He said the company has redirected almost 80% of its engineering capacity towards building cybersecurity defences over the past two quarters. "It is just the reality now."

NIUM Founder and Chief Executive Officer Prajit Nanu also highlighted the risks posed by more advanced AI models, saying the potential for cyberattacks had become a major concern after 11 years of building the payments company.

"Now, with the new AI models, our ability to get hacked is so crazy. It is scary right now," he said during the panel discussion.

Nanu said fintech companies were investing time in strengthening their systems as AI models became increasingly capable.

Addo AI Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Ayesha Khanna said cybersecurity was also a major concern amongst the banks she advises. She pointed to the challenges of securing legacy infrastructure, saying banks could not patch their systems quickly enough.

"There's just so much legacy infrastructure, which is an advantage to the fintechs at the moment, but the speed at which they can patch their systems is limited, and they just can't move fast enough," said Khanna.

She warned that security failures could undermine customer confidence. "And I think that this one mistake can ruin the trust that customers have."

Khanna also cited a cyber incident involving Optimizely, a platform used for A/B testing. She said the incident affected 186 companies and that attackers had sought to access cryptocurrency wallets.

She said the potential loss of customer confidence was a longer-term concern, comparing the consequences to a bank run.

The panel also considered how fintech companies should balance investment in existing businesses with expansion into new areas.

Pine Labs Chief Executive Officer Amrish Rau said that companies should focus on building a strong business in one market rather than spreading themselves too thinly. A profitable core business can provide the resources to fund other opportunities, he said.

Rau also said fintech companies had yet to realise the full potential of their existing markets, with the sector capable of compounding at 25% to 30% over 20 years.

Companies should build on their existing strengths and extend them into newer areas, rather than pursue expansion without a clear strategy.

He cautioned against both refusing to change direction and pivoting too frequently. Companies need to decide whether to invest in new infrastructure or broaden their capabilities into areas such as technology and AI.

Nanu said fintech companies needed to dominate the segments where they had a competitive advantage rather than spread themselves too thinly across markets.

He said NIUM had identified three segments where it believed it could compete effectively and establish itself as a leader, whilst acknowledging that it was less competitive in other markets, such as Africa.

The panel also turned to the security requirements of agentic payments, as AI agents take on a greater role in initiating and executing financial transactions.

When asked which factors would provide a competitive advantage in an agent-driven business environment, Khanna identified trust and execution.

Nanu, however, said deep integration would be important because AI agents would prioritise the fastest and cheapest way to complete transactions.

Shinghal agreed, saying fintech companies needed to understand the parties and underlying activities behind transactions to determine whether they were legitimate.

He said companies needed to go beyond conventional know-your-customer and know-your-business checks to understand individual transactions and the agents involved.

Shinghal said this required gathering information from public and private databases and using transaction-monitoring models to identify suspicious behaviour. He also highlighted the need for compliance, liability, and governance frameworks as agentic payments develop.

He said that the technology enabling communication between AI agents was only a small part of what was needed to make these transactions work securely.
